slides: Open the lecture by naming the central tension of geometric measure theory: geometry wants shapes, while analysis wants quantities stable under limiting processes. The chapter notebook is intentionally modest, so the deck should make the translation guide explicit. Learners should leave the title slide expecting definitions to behave like inspectable contracts, not like decorative vocabulary.

Use this roadmap to prevent the introduction from feeling like a glossary. The course repeatedly passes between algebraic encoding, analytic measurement, geometric tangent data, and topological boundary information. The diagram is deliberately cyclic because the later variational arguments return to the first question: which pieces of geometry remain meaningful after taking limits?

Pause on the notation rather than rushing past it. The important idea is not that Hausdorff measure is already familiar, but that it measures at the dimension of the object being studied. The density term gives room for multiplicity and later for currents. Ask students to identify which part of the notation names the set, the size rule, and the weight.

Emphasize that rectifiability is a repair strategy for rough geometry. A rectifiable object may have corners, overlaps, and omitted bad pieces, but it still has a countable coordinate description in the measure-theoretic sense. The word almost is doing real mathematical work: it identifies which failures are harmless and which failures would break later theorems.

Here the lecture should shift from set geometry to duality. A current remembers an oriented weighted object through all of its form measurements. That sounds abstract, but it is the same move as replacing a vector by its dot products against test vectors. The payoff is that convergence can be discussed by convergence of measurements.

Treat the boundary operator as the first real diagnostic in the lecture. Smooth students know Stokes' theorem as an integral identity; in GMT it becomes a definition that still makes sense for rough oriented objects. The open arc and closed loop illustrate why a finite visual check should always ask what happened to the boundary.

This is the first theorem-orientation slide. The deck does not need the full proof; it needs the meaning of the theorem as a checking device. If the map stretches, the Jacobian compensates. If the map folds, multiplicity compensates. The warning is that a picture of the image alone can erase information that the theorem is designed to preserve.

Make the phrase weak compactness concrete by connecting it to the earlier current slide. A sequence converges if every allowed measurement converges. The hypotheses are not technical decoration: mass control prevents geometric blow-up, and boundary control prevents the limit from solving a different problem. This is the analytic engine behind the later variational applications.

Present this slide as the reason the chapter vocabulary is worth learning. The goal is not merely to define exotic objects, but to create a setting where minimization problems have solutions. The direct method is a compact story: keep the boundary fixed, control mass, take a limit, and use lower semicontinuity to certify that the limit is not worse.

Connect the generated artifact back to the lecture language. The curve is not a copied source figure; it is a durable local model for practicing orientation, perturbation, and diagnostic thinking. Ask learners to identify exactly what the arrows encode and why a finite diagnostic is a miniature promise that the computation remained inside the intended mathematical setup.

Use this as an active diagnostic slide rather than a list of scoldings. Each pitfall corresponds to a later theorem hypothesis: null sets, multiplicity, weak convergence, and boundary constraints. A good classroom move is to ask which pitfall the notebook lab is most likely to expose, then have students justify the answer using the artifact rather than intuition alone.

Close by returning to the notebook's takeaways: concepts become inspectable objects and every visual has a check. The exit exercise is intentionally small, but it asks students to coordinate all four languages at once: set, density, current, and boundary. That coordination is the real prerequisite for reading the later chapters without drowning in notation.
